subject: Critical Thinking
title: The 10/10/10 Rule: Time-Shifting Perspective
description: A fast breakdown of The 10/10/10 Rule: Time-Shifting Perspective for builders.

hook.text: You're angry and about to send a furious email. Ask: How will I feel about this in 10 minutes? 10 months? 10 years?

buildup.text: Suzy Welch's 10/10/10 rule: evaluate decisions across three time horizons to escape the tyranny of the present moment.

discovery.text: It works because emotions are time-bound.

twist.text: Most regrets come from short-term thinking: 'I wish I'd been braver' or 'I wish I'd waited.' 10/10/10 catches these in.

climax.text: For big decisions, the 10-year perspective usually dominates. For small ones, the 10-minute perspective is fine.

punchline.text: Before you decide, time-travel. Future you has better judgment.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 10/10/10 rule?
options: To evaluate decisions across short, medium, and long-term perspectives

details.summary: The 10-10-10 rule asks how you will feel about a decision in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years. This time-shifting technique overcomes short-term emotional reactions by forcing you to consider long-term consequences.
details.whyItMatters: Most regretted decisions are driven by short-term emotions. The 10-10-10 rule provides instant emotional distance and long-term perspective.
takeaways: Short-term emotions often dominate decision making
Time-shifting reveals which consequences truly matter
Suzy Welch popularized the framework for everyday decisions

faq.question: How do you apply the 10-10-10 rule to a difficult personal decision?
faq.answer: Ask yourself: how will I feel about this choice in 10 minutes? In 10 months? In 10 years? If the short-term answer conflicts with the long-term one, the long-term perspective usually reflects your real values better.

faq.question: What types of decisions benefit most from the 10-10-10 framework?
faq.answer: Decisions where you feel strong immediate emotion: confronting a colleague, making a large purchase, ending a relationship. These are situations where short-term feelings are most likely to override long-term interests.
